A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\phi\in H^k$ is any other representer, then for every $s\in\mathcal T$ and coordinate $j$, $\langle\phi_j-\phi_{0,j},s\rangle_H=0$, so $\phi_j-\phi_{0,j}\in\mathcal T^\perp$ by [F3]. Thus every representer lies in $\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$.

Apply [F2] coordinatewise to write $\phi_0=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0+h$ with $\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0\in\mathcal T^k$ and $h\in(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$. Countable Choice is used only in this projection step through [F2] and [A1].

Conversely, if $h\in(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$, then $\langle\phi_0+h,s\rangle_H=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H+\langle h,s\rangle_H=\dot\psi(s)$ for every $s\in\mathcal T$, so $\phi_0+h$ is a representer. Hence the full representer set is exactly the stated affine class.

By step 1.2, $\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$ is a representer. If two representers lie in $\mathcal T^k$, step 1.1 places their difference in $(\mathcal T^\perp)^k$ as well; each coordinate then lies in $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal T^\perp$ and has squared norm zero by positive definiteness in [F1], so the difference is zero. This proves existence and uniqueness of the canonical representer.

Let $\theta\in\mathbb R^p$, $p\ge1$ finite, be a parameter of interest at a law $P$. Assume its score vector $S_\theta=(S_{\theta,1},\ldots,S_{\theta,p})^T$ has components in $L^2_0(P)$; under a dominated differentiable parametric submodel these are the coordinate log-density scores of [[def-score-and-fisher-information]]. Let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be the closed nuisance tangent space of [[def-nuisance-tangent-space]]. The ambient $L^2_0(P)$ is as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The score-density convention uses the Axiom of Choice, while Hilbert projection uses Countable Choice; both dependencies are retained separately.

The Hilbert decomposition [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] defines $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}f$ as the unique $g\in\mathcal T_\eta$ with $f-g\in\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$, where orthogonality and $\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$ have the meanings in [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **efficient score vector** and **efficient information matrix** are

$$S_{\mathrm{eff}}=S_\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}S_\theta,\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T],$$

where $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}$ is the Hilbert-space orthogonal projection applied coordinatewise. This projection exists and is unique because $\mathcal T_\eta$ is a closed linear subspace; the projection theorem used by [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be a closed linear subspace, and let $\dot\psi:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous linear with an ambient representer $\phi_0\in H^k$, meaning $\dot\psi(s)=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H$ coordinatewise for all $s\in\mathcal T$. Assume Countable Choice. Then all ambient representers are exactly

$$\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k.$$

The unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$ is $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$; when $\dot\psi$ is a statistical path derivative, this is its canonical gradient. Projection is applied coordinatewise.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$ be any tangent set in the real Hilbert space $L^2_0(P)$. Its tangent space $\mathcal T(P)$, defined as the norm closure of its finite real linear span ([[def-tangent-space]]), is a closed linear subspace of $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space. Vectors $x,y\in V$ are
**orthogonal**, written $x\perp y$, when

$$\langle x,y\rangle=0 .$$

For a subset $S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^\perp:=\{\,v\in V : \langle v,s\rangle=0 \text{ for every } s\in S\,\}.$$

**Orthogonality is symmetric.** If $\langle x,y\rangle=0$, then
$\langle y,x\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}=0$, so $x\perp y$ exactly
when $y\perp x$; in particular the condition defining $S^\perp$ is symmetric in
its two arguments.

**$S^\perp$ is a linear subspace.** Let $s\in S$ and scalars $a,b$; then
$\langle 0,s\rangle=0$, and if $u,v\in S^\perp$ then
$\langle au+bv,s\rangle=a\langle u,s\rangle+b\langle v,s\rangle=0$ by linearity
in the first argument, so $au+bv\in S^\perp$. Thus $S^\perp$ is a linear
subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]) for every subset $S$, whether or not
$S$ is a subspace. Moreover $0\in S^\perp$ always, and $v\in V$ lies in
$\{0\}^\perp$ for every $v$, so $\{0\}^\perp=V$.

**Monotonicity.** If $S\subseteq T\subseteq V$, then every vector orthogonal to
all of $T$ is orthogonal to all of $S$, so $T^\perp\subseteq S^\perp$.

**Nontriviality of orthogonality.** By positive definiteness
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2=0$ exactly for $v=0$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]),
so a vector orthogonal to itself is zero, and $\{0\}^\perp=V$, $V^\perp=\{0\}$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By the orthogonal-projection definition in [F1] and [F7], $R\in\mathcal T_\eta^p$ and each coordinate of $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is orthogonal to every element of $\mathcal T_\eta$ by [F8]. Since $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq\mathcal T$, both $S_\theta$ and $R$ belong to $\mathcal T^p$, hence $S_{\mathrm{eff}}\in\mathcal T^p$. The projection exists by the Hilbert and closed-subspace hypotheses [F5] and [F6] under [A2]; [A1] is carried through the selected score definition.

Because $S_\theta=S_{\mathrm{eff}}+R$ and $R$ is nuisance-tangent-valued, orthogonality [F8] gives $E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_\theta^T]=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Therefore for every $a\in\mathbb R^p$ and $t\in\mathcal T_\eta$, $E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}(a^TS_\theta+t)]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}a$.

If $a^TS_\theta+t=a'^TS_\theta+t'$ for $t,t'\in\mathcal T_\eta$, step 2.1 applied to the difference gives $I_{\mathrm{eff}}(a-a')=0$. Nonsingularity forces $a=a'$, so the target derivative assigned to a score in the allowed score set is well-defined.

Set $\phi=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}$. For a score $s=a^TS_\theta+t$, step 2.1 gives $E_P[\phi s]=a$. Moreover $\phi\in\mathcal T^p$ by step 1.1 and [F4]. The map $s\mapsto E_P[\phi s]$ is continuous in $L^2(P)$ by [F9], so it extends uniquely from the dense allowed score set to $\mathcal T$ and agrees there with the path derivative. Thus $\phi$ is a representer in the full tangent space.

By [F3], a representer in $\mathcal T^p$ is the unique canonical gradient, so $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The second-moment matrix $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is symmetric, hence so is its inverse. Direct multiplication gives $E_P[\phi\phi^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}I_{\mathrm{eff}}I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$. No existence of an estimator is used.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by

derivations.claim: For $r>1$ and $k\ge2$, monotonicity gives $k^{-r}\le\int_{k-1}^k x^{-r}dx$, so $\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-r}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-r}dx<\infty$. Taking $r=3$ shows $c$ is well-defined and the displayed masses sum to one; taking $r=2$ gives $\mu=c\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<\infty$, so $P\in\mathcal M_X$. But $E_PX^2=c\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1}=\infty$, because each dyadic block $2^{j-1}<k\le2^j$ contributes at least $1/2$.

For bounded centered $s$, choose $t\ge0$ small enough that $1+ts\ge0$. By [F7], $E_P(1+ts)=1$, so [F9] gives a probability law $P_{t,s}$ with density $1+ts$. The identity $\sqrt{1+u}-1-u/2=-u^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+u})^2]$ bounds the square-root remainder for $u=ts$ in $L^2(P)$ by $t^2\|s^2\|_2/2=o(t)$, since $s$ is bounded. Thus these paths are DQM with score $s$ under [F1]. To see their scores are dense in $L^2_0(P)$, take $g\in L^2_0(P)$ and truncate to $g_m=\max(-m,\min(g,m))$. Dominated convergence gives $g_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$ because $|g_m-g|^2\le g^2$ and the difference tends pointwise to zero. Cauchy--Schwarz and $\|1\|_2=1$ give $E_Pg_m\to0$, so $g_m-E_Pg_m$ are bounded centered scores converging to $g$. Hence the tangent space is $L^2_0(P)$.

Step 1.1 gives $P\in\mathcal M_X$ and $E_PX<\infty$; since $s$ is bounded, [F8] gives the finite expectation $E_{P_{t,s}}X=E_P[X(1+ts)]$, so every designated path lies in $\mathcal M_X$. Linearity [F7] then gives $\psi(P_{t,s})=E_{P_{t,s}}X=\mu+tE_P[Xs]$, so the right derivative on each allowed score is $\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[Xs]$.

For $m\ge2$ let $s_m=(X\wedge m)-E_P[X\wedge m]$. These are bounded centered scores. Their norms are positive because $X\wedge m$ takes the distinct values $1$ and $2$ on the positive-mass points $k=1$ and $k=2$. Direct summation gives $E_P[Xs_m]=cH_m+cm\sum_{k>m}k^{-2}-\mu E_P[X\wedge m]\ge cH_m-\mu^2$, since $0\le X\wedge m\le X$. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

derivations.claim: Since $X\in L^2(P)$ and $P$ is a probability, Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] gives $\mu=E_PX<\infty$. For bounded centered $s$ and sufficiently small $t\ge0$, $1+ts\ge0$ and $E_P(1+ts)=1+tE_Ps=1$, so $P_{t,s}$ is a probability law with density $1+ts$ by [F9]. Direct rationalization gives $\sqrt{1+u}-1-u/2=-u^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+u})^2]$; for $u=ts$ the $L^2(P)$ norm of the DQM remainder in [F10] is at most $t^2\|s^2\|_2/2=o(t)$ because $s$ is bounded. Thus the score is $s$.

Every bounded mean-zero $s$ is an allowed score. If $g\in L^2_0(P)$, truncate it to $g_m=\max(-m,\min(g,m))$. Then $g_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$ by [F6], since $|g_m-g|^2\le g^2$ and the difference tends pointwise to zero. Also $E_Pg_m\to E_Pg=0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and [F3], [F5]. Hence $s_m=g_m-E_Pg_m$ is bounded and mean-zero, and $s_m\to g$ in $L^2(P)$. Thus the score closure is exactly $L^2_0(P)$ by the tangent-space convention [F10].

Since $P\in\mathcal M_X$, $E_PX<\infty$; with bounded $s$, [F8] gives the finite expectation $E_{P_{t,s}}X=E_P[X(1+ts)]$, so every designated path lies in $\mathcal M_X$. Linearity [F7] then yields $\psi(P_{t,s})=E_{P_{t,s}}X=\mu+tE_P[Xs]$. Since $E_Ps=0$, the right derivative is $E_P[(X-\mu)s]$.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|E_P[(X-\mu)s]|\le\|X-\mu\|_2\|s\|_2$, so the derivative extends continuously to $\mathcal T$. The vector $X-\mu$ is mean-zero and square-integrable, hence belongs to $\mathcal T$. If another $\tilde\varphi\in\mathcal T$ represents the same derivative, then $h=\tilde\varphi-(X-\mu)\in\mathcal T$ is orthogonal to every bounded mean-zero score; by density and continuity it is orthogonal to itself, so $E_Ph^2=0$ and $h=0$. By [F10], $X-\mu$ is the unique representer in $\mathcal T$ and therefore the canonical gradient.

By the empirical-measure convention in [F2] and $E_P(X-\mu)=0$, $(P_n-P)(X-\mu)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X(X_i)-\mu)=\overline X_n-\mu$ exactly. Step 2.1 gives $X-\mu\in L^2_0(P)$. The remainder is zero, so the sample mean is asymptotically linear with estimator influence function $X-\mu$ under [F2]. This algebraic identity invokes no central limit theorem.

Let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq L^2_0(P)$ be the closed nuisance tangent space of [[def-nuisance-tangent-space]]. The ambient $L^2_0(P)$ is as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The score-density convention uses the Axiom of Choice, while Hilbert projection uses Countable Choice; both dependencies are retained separately.

The Hilbert decomposition [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] defines $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}f$ as the unique $g\in\mathcal T_\eta$ with $f-g\in\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$, where orthogonality and $\mathcal T_\eta^\perp$ have the meanings in [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. The **efficient score vector** and **efficient information matrix** are

$$S_{\mathrm{eff}}=S_\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}S_\theta,\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T],$$

where $\Pi_{\mathcal T_\eta}$ is the Hilbert-space orthogonal projection applied coordinatewise. This projection exists and is unique because $\mathcal T_\eta$ is a closed linear subspace; the projection theorem used by [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. $$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure
$\mu$, and let $p_\theta$ be selected finite-valued measurable
Radon–Nikodym density representatives as in
[[def-likelihood-density]]. The simultaneous selection of this arbitrary-index
family uses the Axiom of Choice. No measurability of $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$
or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$ is
implied.

Let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at
which the selected family $\eta\mapsto p_\eta(x)$ is differentiable for
$\mu$-almost every $x$, with measurable coordinate derivatives. On
$\{x:p_\theta(x)>0\}$, define the log-likelihood
$\ell_\theta(x)=\log p_\theta(x)$ and the **score**
$$S_\theta(x):=\nabla_\theta\ell_\theta(x) =\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_j}\log p_\theta(x)\right)_{j=1}^d.$$
Set $S_\theta(x)=0$ where $p_\theta(x)=0$, which is $P_\theta$-null.
For $d=1$, this is $S_\theta=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta$.

For $d=1$, the scalar **Fisher information** is
$$I(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
When $d>1$ and $S_\theta$ is square-integrable, the **Fisher information
matrix** is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[S_\theta(X)S_\theta(X)^\mathsf T]$;
its $i,j$ entry is $\mathbb E_\theta[S_{\theta,i}S_{\theta,j}]$. No scalar
information is defined here for a vector parameter.
The information matrix is a second-moment matrix by definition; it equals the
score covariance matrix when the score has mean zero.

The derivatives, score and information are defined relative to the specified
differentiable representative family. The Radon–Nikodym definition alone
does not supply parameter differentiability or a canonical score version.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $H=L^2_0(P)$, let $S_\theta\in H^p$ be a finite-dimensional interest-score vector, and let $\mathcal T_\eta\subseteq\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be closed linear nuisance and full tangent spaces, with $\mathcal T_\eta$ a subspace of $\mathcal T$. Assume the designated allowed score set is exactly

$$\mathcal S=\{a^TS_\theta+t:a\in\mathbb R^p,\ t\in\mathcal T_\eta\},\qquad \mathcal T=\overline{\mathcal S}^{\,L^2(P)},$$

and every allowed one-sided path with score $a^TS_\theta+t\in\mathcal S$ has right target derivative $a$ for the parameter $\theta$. If $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_P[S_{\mathrm{eff}}S_{\mathrm{eff}}^T]$ is nonsingular, then $\theta$ is pathwise differentiable and its canonical gradient is

$$\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$

Its covariance matrix is $E_P[\phi_{\mathrm{can}}\phi_{\mathrm{can}}^T]=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$. This theorem does not assert that an estimator attaining the covariance bound exists.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each parameter in the stated domain, $|\theta(u+v)+\eta u|\le2|\theta|+|\eta|<1$, so each mass is positive. Their sum is one because $\sum_{u,v}(u+v)=\sum_{u,v}u=0$ and the four constant terms sum to four. Thus the family consists of probability laws by [F5].

Finite averaging, using [F6], gives $E_PU=E_PV=0$, $E_PU^2=E_PV^2=1$, and $E_PUV=0$. Thus $w=a(U+V)+bU$ is bounded and centered. Along $(\theta_t,\eta_t)=(at,bt)$ the likelihood ratio is $1+tw$, which is nonnegative and integrates to one for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. The square-root identity $\sqrt{1+z}-1-z/2=-z^2/[2(1+\sqrt{1+z})^2]$ gives an $L^2(P)$ remainder bounded by $t^2\|w^2\|_2/2=o(t)$, so the path is DQM with score $w$ by [F2]. Direct differentiation of the log density gives interest score $U+V$ and nuisance score $U$ by [F3]. Thus the designated nuisance scores span $\{U\}$, which is closed since $\|cU\|_2=|c|$, and all designated scores $a(U+V)+bU$ span $\{U,V\}$, which is closed because $\|aU+bV\|_2^2=a^2+b^2$.

Since $U\in\mathcal T_\eta$ and $E_P[(U+V-U)U]=E_P[VU]=0$, $U$ is the orthogonal projection of $S_\theta=U+V$ onto $\mathcal T_\eta$. Hence $S_{\mathrm{eff}}=V$ and $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_PV^2=1$ by [F1].
